Introduction

Broadly speaking, the acoustics most of us know, and physical acoustics in particular, studies the vibration of macroscopic objects and the way those vibrations travel through macroscopic media. By solving the wave equation, a partial differential equation, under all kinds of conditions, we obtain a whole zoo of sound-wave solutions and study their properties. Vibrating objects and sound are part of everyday life, so the study of acoustics goes back to before the Common Era. Condensed matter physics, by contrast, was born only after quantum mechanics gave us a description of the microscopic world. The arrival of quantum mechanics in the twentieth century immediately opened up two lines of work. One went deeper into the microscopic world to probe the secrets inside the atom, and eventually grew into particle physics and high-energy physics. The other was reductionist: it hoped to explain the properties of macroscopic objects, such as the electrical and thermal conductivity of solids, from the laws that govern microscopic particles, and it grew into condensed matter physics. (Although the very existence of condensed matter physics is, at heart, a huge irony at reductionism’s expense.) The two fields seem to have nothing whatsoever to do with each other. Yet while leafing through papers recently, I noticed that some researchers are trying to explore new approaches to condensed matter physics from the acoustic side, or drawing on concepts from condensed matter to help with acoustics research. So I decided to introduce this curious marriage of the macroscopic and the microscopic here, for your enjoyment.

Topological structure in solid materials

I suspect most readers of this article know more about acoustics, so in this section I will first lay some groundwork by introducing a few basic concepts from condensed matter physics, as simply as I can.

1. The periodicity of crystals

Taken literally, condensed matter physics describes matter in a “condensed” state. Matter generally comes in three states, solid, liquid and gas, and the two that deserve the word “condensed” are liquids and solids. In practice, condensed matter physics is mostly concerned with the properties of solids, and only occasionally with those of special liquids (such as superfluid liquid helium, which exhibits a macroscopic quantum state). Among all the solids, condensed matter physics pays particular attention to a class of materials called crystals. What sets crystals apart is that their atoms (or ions) are arranged with a regular periodicity. Take ordinary table salt, a crystal of sodium chloride: Figure 1 shows how sodium and chloride ions alternate in a periodic arrangement inside the salt crystal.

Figure 1. Arrangement of ions in a sodium chloride crystal (image from the internet)

Sodium chloride has one of the simpler arrangements among crystals; some metal oxides can be arranged in far more complex ways. But however the atoms are arranged, there is always some kind of periodicity, and this periodicity, or put another way, this symmetry, is the core of the theoretical framework of condensed matter physics.

2. Electronic energy bands

Anyone with middle-school chemistry will remember that an atom (or ion) consists of a nucleus at the center and electrons around it, and that the electrons are arranged in shells, or energy levels, according to their energy. In chemical reactions, the low-energy inner electrons stay put; the ones that atoms actually fight over are the high-energy valence electrons in the outer shell.

Figure 2. Electron configuration (valence electrons usually come from the outermost shell, and very occasionally from the next shell in or deeper; image from the internet)

In condensed matter physics, these valence electrons are the particles we care about most, because a crystal’s electrical and thermal conductivity, and even its magnetism, all come from them. Being high in energy, the valence electrons in a crystal sit relatively far from the nucleus they originally belong to, so they inevitably feel the pull of other nuclei nearby. In more physical language, the potential a valence electron sits in can no longer be approximated as coming from a single nucleus; all the nuclei in the crystal have to be considered together. In other words, the potential felt by valence electrons in a crystal is a periodic potential, because the atoms in a crystal are arranged periodically.

Figure 3. Schematic of the electron distribution in a crystal (image from the internet)

Some of you may point out that, besides the positively charged nuclei, an electron also feels the other negatively charged valence electrons. This touches on the notoriously thorny problem of electron–electron interactions in condensed matter. Put simply, if the concentration of valence electrons is low, the interaction can be neglected or handled with a mean-field approximation, and we can still treat each valence electron as moving in a periodic potential. If the concentration is so high that the interaction can no longer be neglected, there is, at the current stage of the field, no standard way of dealing with it, and many problems remain open. In short, it is an extremely hard and extremely important hot topic. But it is not what I want to discuss here, so we can safely set it aside for now.

So how do we describe an electron moving in a periodic potential? Quantum mechanics tells us that, much as in the potential of a single nucleus (a central potential), electrons moving in a periodic potential form a series of energy bands, ordered by energy:

Figure 4. Schematic of energy bands (image from the internet)

As the rightmost panel of the figure shows, going from low to high energy, each band is, strictly speaking, made up of many closely spaced energy levels, roughly as many as there are atoms in the crystal. Because they are packed so densely, each band can be treated as a quasi-continuous spectrum. The gaps between bands are called forbidden bands, because the Schrödinger equation has no eigenstate solutions for an electron wave function with an energy inside them. In other words, an electron with an energy in a forbidden band cannot exist stably in the crystal and will inevitably make a transition to a neighboring band. The width of a forbidden band is called the band gap. As in an atom, electrons fill the bands from the bottom up, and the highest band they fill is called the valence band. The empty band above the valence band is called the empty band or the conduction band. (I know that by now “band” has probably stopped looking like a real word to you, lol.)

In fact, an electron’s energy depends not only on which band it is in but also on its momentum. The relationship between energy and momentum is called the dispersion relation. Experimentally measured band structures of crystals usually look like Figure 5:

Figure 5. Schematic band structure (image from the internet)

A real band structure ought to be four-dimensional, because momentum is a vector. Three dimensions of momentum plus one of energy would need four dimensions to show in full, which is plainly impossible to draw. To simplify the picture while still showing as much of the band behavior as possible, we pick particular directions and magnitudes of momentum (the horizontal axis above) and plot the bands along them; that is the figure above. Each curve represents the dispersion relation of one energy level, or one state, that electrons can occupy. Although each band is quasi-continuous, we draw only a few representative dispersion curves per band here. The figure shows a clear gap between the conduction band and the valence band: the forbidden band. The material in Figure 5 would generally be an insulator, because its Fermi level, the highest level the electrons fill up to, sits right at the top of the valence band. Valence electrons there are hard to accelerate with an external electric field, so current does not flow easily. (Acceleration means an increase in energy, but directly above the electrons at the top of the band lies the forbidden band, so they have no way to gain energy unless they jump across the gap, and such a transition generally takes more energy than an external field can supply.) In a conductor, the Fermi level lies within the conduction band, so the topmost valence electrons are easily accelerated by an external field and a current flows. This is a very simple but very meaningful application of band theory.

About the author: jemand graduated in physics from Nanjing University and is now studying for a master’s in physics at RWTH Aachen University. Will probably end up working on something to do with acoustics. That’s all.
